units.translation: Thus Wunderlich p. 27 for αντέστη [opposed], but the structure of the words is perverse: ὃς ἀνέστη συρίζων φόνον πᾶσιν θεοῖς σμερδναῖσι γαμφηλαῖσι [who rose up hissing slaughter against all the gods with terrible jaws]. The datives πᾶσιν θεοῖς [to all the gods] depend on ἀνέστη [rose up]. Thus Homer Il. 23, 634 πὺς μὲν ἐνίκησα Κλυτομήδεα, Ηνοπος υἱόν, | Αγκαῖον δὲ πάλη Πλευρώνιον, ὅς μοι ἀνέστη [In boxing I defeated Clytomedes, son of Enops, and in wrestling Ancaeus of Pleuron, who rose up against me]. When Aristides quotes this in vol. 2 p. 503, in a certain Florentine manuscript ἀντέστη [opposed] is written with the same error.

[καὶ νύκτα ταύτην ἣν λέγεις ἐπ᾽ ἀσπίδος ἄστροισι μαρμαίρουσαν οὐρανοῦ κυρεῖν τάχ᾽ ἂν γένοιτο μάντις ἡ ἄνοιά τινι [And this night which you speak of, gleaming with stars on the shield, might soon be a prophet of heaven to someone, the folly]. Thus M, where the corrector wrote ἡ ἀνοία [the folly], about which the scholium says: παροξυτόνως Αττικῶς ἀντὶ τοῦ ἄνοια· διὰ δὲ τὸ μέτρον ἐξέτεινεν [with acute accent on the penult, in Attic fashion, instead of ἄνοια [folly]; and for the sake of the meter he lengthened it], which annotation, like many others, was undoubtedly written by the corrector himself after he had corrected ἀνοία [folly] in the text, not noticing the fraud of the old interpolator, who, not understanding that the subject of the verb is νύξ [night], which is contained in the words καὶ νύκτα ταύτην ἣν λέγεις [and this night which you speak of], said for metrical reasons by attraction instead of καὶ ἡ νύξ αὕτη ἣν λέγεις [and this night which you speak of], foolishly wrote ἡ ἄνοια [the folly] (or ἀνοία [folly]) and added τινί [to someone], which is utterly alien to this passage. I, as the sense demanded, restored τάχ᾽ ἂν γένοιτο μάντις οἷα πείσεται [soon might become a prophet of what he will suffer]. In the older scholium, taking no account of that ἡ ἀνοία τινί [the folly to someone], these words are correctly explained thus: τάχα προμαντεύεται τῷ φοροῦντι ὅτι χωρήσει ὑπό νύκτα [soon it prophesies to the bearer that he will advance under cover of night].]
